To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the police reform process was a complex, multi-actor and multi-level process that involved the adaptation of the international community, the European Union and local actors, and the resistance to change of the international community and the European Union.
the police restructuring process was influenced by a combination of adaptation and (re)active resistance techniques employed by key actors in the process.

(1) the EU was not able to implement the police reform process according to its original plans; (2) this was due to the resistance of key actors in the police reform process; and (3) the final outcome was a result of a combination of adaptation and muddling-through techniques employed by key actors in the reform process, including international, European and Bosnian actors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of why and how certain practices, routines and positions of actors influence the outcome and timing of police reform.
the question of how and why specific actors, practices and routines influence the outcome of the police reform process in Bosnia.
how the European Union and its member states have influenced the police restructuring process and how the police reform process has in turn influenced the European Union.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the police restructuring process was not only a process of ‘reform’, but also a process of ‘(Re)turn’ and (re)adaptation to a functionalist model.
, in the case of police reform, the European Union was able to achieve its main objectives of establishing a police service that would be accountable and transparent.
the police restructuring process was not a failure, but that it was a success in a very particular way: it was a ‘muddle-through’ success.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the EU, in its role as a key actor in police reform, has been successful in achieving its main goals, namely to create a police service which can be integrated into the EU and to contribute to the stability and security of the region.
the police restructuring process was a result of a complex process of ‘muddle through’ in which the EU was a central, but by no means the only, actor.
the European Union, through its police reform activities, has become a ‘field of practice’ in its own right.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the police reform in Bosnia was not a failure, but rather a process that was shaped by the interaction between different actors’ preferences and strategies.

the police reform process in Bosnia was a complex process of adaptation and resistance, which was not a simple top-down imposition of the international community, but a complex interaction between local, international and EU actors.
SSR should be understood as a field of practice that is influenced by a combination of adaptation and resistant techniques, which can lead to a process of ‘ muddling through ’.
